result.summary: Pausanias describes the Phocian towns along the Cephisus: Ledon, Lilaea, Charadra, the lost Parapotamii, Amphiclea, Tithronium and Drymaea. He gives distances, temples, local legends and histories of destruction.

scenes.title: Ledon and its ruin
scenes.summary: The road from Tithorea leads to deserted Ledon, whose remnant settles by the Cephisus. Pausanias compares its ruin to other towns destroyed by wrongdoing.

scenes.title: Lilaea and Charadra
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Lilaea's history, buildings, river and climate, then nearby Charadra.
scenes.stakes: The town of Lilaea is besieged and garrisoned by Philip's Macedonians until Patron leads a rising.

scenes.title: Parapotamii and the Cephisus land
scenes.summary: Pausanias discusses the fertile Cephisus land and Homer's line, and the vanished town of Parapotamii.

scenes.title: Amphiclea and the snake
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the names of Amphiclea and the tale of the child, wolf and snake, then the Dionysus rites.
scenes.stakes: A ruler's baby son is threatened by a wolf and then mistakenly killed by his father.

scenes.title: Tithronium and Drymaea
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes Tithronium, Apollo's grove, and Drymaea with its founder and temple of Demeter.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title of Demeter at Drymaea (Thesmophoros).

analysis.text: Pausanias links towns' fates to moral causes, such as impiety and wrongdoing, alongside local legends of naming.
The passage records Phocian ruin after the Sacred War and Persian and Macedonian attacks, as well as local cults.

language_notes.text: The Phocian General Council was the common assembly of the Phocian cities, to which even small settlements like this one sent representatives.
An Autochthon is a person said to have sprung from the soil of the land itself, a native with no immigrant ancestry.
Paris carried off Menelaus' wife Helen, which caused the Trojan War. Hestiæus of Miletus helped provoke the Ionian revolt against Persia.
Philomelus was the Phocian general who seized Delphi's sanctuary in the Sacred War (356 BC), an act of impiety; Phocian towns were later punished.
"Capitulated upon conditions of war" means surrendered on agreed terms, not unconditionally; the same phrase later describes the Macedonians' own terms of withdrawal.
Pentelican marble comes from Mount Pentelicus near Athens and was prized for fine sculpture.
Naiades (Naiads) are nymphs of springs, rivers and lakes.
A quotation from Homer's Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad, listing the Phocian contingents at Troy.
The Amphictyones were the league of neighbouring peoples who administered Delphi and the Pythian Games, held in honour of Apollo.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet, so 60 stades is about seven miles.
"Orgies" here means secret religious rites, not the modern sense of debauchery.
The ellipsis marks a gap or corruption in the text; the sentence is incomplete and the citation of Herodotus is uncertain.
"Law-giving Demeter" is the goddess's title Thesmophoros; her festival, the Thesmophoria, was celebrated by women.

context_notes.text: Philip V of Macedon, son of Demetrius II, was king in the late third and early second century BC and campaigned in central Greece.
Delphi was the usual place for Greek cities to set up statues honouring benefactors.
Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, were twin heroes, brothers of Helen, widely honoured in Greece.
Xerxes, king of Persia, invaded Greece in 480 BC and burned Phocian towns on his march, as Herodotus records.
After the Sacred War (346 BC), the Amphictyones decreed the destruction of Phocian towns as punishment for seizing Delphi's treasury.
Dream-oracles and healing were typical of cults of healing gods; here Dionysus is credited with them, and the priest prophesies in possession.
Phocus, son of Æacus, was the legendary eponymous founder of the Phocians, and half-brother of Peleus and Telamon.

literary_notes.text: Famous disasters, Troy and Miletus, serve as parallels, framing Ledon's fall as part of a broader moral pattern.
"Wiped off the face of the globe" pictures destruction as erasing a mark, stressing how complete the ruin was.
The river's midday noise is compared to a bull's roar, giving a vivid sense of its violence near the source.
The father kills the snake that saved his child, and the child too, through a tragic misreading of appearances.
The tale explains a place-name and a landscape feature by a legend, a common technique in Pausanias.
Pausanias's reserved tone, calling the rites noteworthy yet describing them only by absence, shows his religious caution before mysteries.
